title: Re-flooding the Mesopotamian marshes
place: Chibaish and the Hammar Marsh, southern Iraq
mode_reason: A bounded act in 2003, residents breaking the dikes that kept the rivers out, brought water back to about 75 percent of the pre-drainage level by 2008; the source also shows the gain does not hold by itself when river flow falls.
who: Returning marsh residents such as Amjad Mohamed, who hacked at the dikes in 2003, and a small group of environmentalists led by Azzam Alwash of Nature Iraq.
does: They breached the dikes built under Saddam Hussein so the Tigris and Euphrates could refill the drained wetlands.
pays: not stated
result: 'From a high of around 75 percent restored in 2008, the wetlands are now at 58 percent of their average pre-drained level' and expected to fall below 50 percent that summer (National Geographic, July 2015; the measuring body is not named). Salinity reached 15,000 ppm in some areas, up from 300 to 500 ppm in the 1980s.
contested: The recovery is weaker than its reputation. A Swansea University-led study of satellite data for 2000 to 2023 found gains 'repeatedly interrupted by severe declines', the worst in 2008-2009 and 2022-2023, and that upstream river flow, not local rain, controls the marsh (https://www.swansea.ac.uk/press-office/news-events/news/2026/07/researchers-reveal-why-river-management-is-so-crucial-to-protecting-one-of-worlds-most-important-wetlands.php). Dams in Turkey and Iran have cut the rivers' combined volume by up to 60 percent, according to the UN as cited by National Geographic.
when_it_stops: Documented: when upstream flow drops the marsh shrinks and turns salty; fishers and buffalo herders report halved milk yields and poor catches (2015).
quote: The water's just bad. It's so salty, it's not like it was before
quote_speaker: Amjad Mohamed, fisherman who helped break the dikes in 2003 and later left again for Basra
source_title: Iraq's Famed Marshes Are Disappearing—Again
notes: Saved: iraq_natgeo.txt, iraq_swansea.txt. Mode is a judgment call: the 2003 act was bounded, but the marsh now depends on continuing water releases upstream, which is closer to 'repeats' at the level of river management. title: Rinderpest: the cattle plague ended
mode_reason: The virus was last seen in buffalo in Meru National Park in October 2001, vaccination was deliberately ceased, and FAO and OIE declared global eradication in 2011.
who: Community-based animal health workers, 'livestock owners selected by their communities', alongside national veterinary services, NGOs and FAO; the source names a community worker from Karamoja, Uganda, who identified an outbreak.
does: Carried heat-stable vaccine on foot, by bicycle or by animal to pastoral herds, vaccinated cattle, and reported outbreaks through participatory disease searching.
pays: Pan-African Rinderpest Campaign 'supported largely by the European Commission'; the earlier JP15 campaign by USAID and other aid programmes (as the source states).

title: Guinea worm: the last villages
mode_reason: The campaign aims at a permanent zero with no vaccine or medicine (10 human cases in 2025 against an estimated 3.5 million a year in 1986), but it has not turned yet and Chad shows it can reverse.

title: Measles returns to Samoa
mode_reason: Protection lasted only while each cohort of infants was vaccinated: when coverage fell to rates 'as low as 31%', measles infected 5707 people within months.
who: Hospital and district nurses who vaccinate at clinics and in home visits from a Ministry of Health minivan; village women's committees historically supported immunisation.

pays: Ministry of Health; UNICEF worked in Samoa during the outbreak (amounts not stated).

The year of the infant deaths (2018) is from memory; the article gives no year. The 31% figure is reported as what was 'blamed'. A WHO outbreak-notice URL tried from memory turned out to be about polio.

title: Canada loses measles elimination status
mode_reason: Elimination was verified, then lost: PAHO found endemic transmission re-established in Canada after at least 12 months of circulation, with regional second-dose coverage at 79% against the 95% needed.
who: Not described in the source beyond national health authorities and PAHO technical teams; the routine work is childhood MMR vaccination, surveillance and outbreak response.
does: Two-dose MMR vaccination of each birth cohort, case surveillance, laboratory confirmation and rapid outbreak response.
pays: not stated
result: As of 7 November 2025: 12,596 confirmed cases in ten countries of the Americas, a 30-fold increase on 2024, and 28 deaths; more than 5,000 confirmed cases in Canada since October 2024 (PAHO).
contested: PAHO's director called the loss 'a setback' but 'reversible'; the source notes earlier temporary losses in Venezuela (2018) and Brazil (2019), with regional status regained in 2024 and lost again within about a year.
when_it_stops: 89% of cases were in unvaccinated people or those of unknown status; transmission 'primarily affected under-vaccinated communities', and the whole Region of the Americas lost its measles-free verification.
quote: This loss represents a setback—but it is also reversible
quote_speaker: Dr Jarbas Barbosa, Director, Pan American Health Organization
source_title: PAHO calls for regional action as the Americas lose measles elimination status
notes: Saved: canada_measles_paho.txt. No front-line worker appears in the source; a Canadian public-health or local news source would be needed to make them visible. The 79% coverage figure is the regional average for 2024, not Canada's. Pin is the province centroid.

title: Wolbachia mosquitoes in Yogyakarta
mode_reason: Mosquitoes were released for several months in 2017 only; the bacterium spreads itself through the wild population and the implementer reports it still at a very high level more than three years after releases ended.
who: Researchers at Universitas Gadjah Mada and the World Mosquito Program, with residents who hosted release containers and a community reference group; leaders of 37 urban villages gave consent.
does: Placed containers of Wolbachia-carrying mosquito eggs in a minority of homes for 9 to 14 rounds per area, then monitored with 348 traps.
pays: Tahija Foundation (trial funder); sponsor Universitas Gadjah Mada.
result: Cluster-randomised trial: confirmed dengue in 2.3% of participants in treated areas against 9.4% in untreated, protective efficacy 77.1% (95% CI 65.3 to 84.9); hospitalisation efficacy 86.2% (Utarini et al., NEJM 2021).
contested: It has not held everywhere: in Rio de Janeiro only 32% of mosquitoes on average carried the strain and dengue fell 38% (https://europepmc.org/article/PMC/PMC9630156); a 2026 paper reports levels still sub-optimal 30 months after a decline linked to a larvicide switch, and notes heat can destabilise the strain (https://europepmc.org/article/PMC/PMC13645213).
when_it_stops: Releases are meant to stop. In Yogyakarta the trial found only areas above 80% Wolbachia frequency were protected; where frequency fell, as in Rio, protection was modest.
quote: We have welcomed this project to our community.
quote_speaker: Mrs Riyan, Yogyakarta resident and head of the trial's Community Reference Group
source_title: Efficacy of Wolbachia-Infected Mosquito Deployments for the Control of Dengue
source_publisher: New England Journal of Medicine (author manuscript via Europe PMC)
notes: Saved: wolbachia_nejm_utarini2021.txt, wmp_rct_release.txt, wolbachia_rio_lancetid2022.txt, wolbachia_rio_mioc2026.txt, yogya_vice.txt. The quote and the 'three years' persistence claim come from the World Mosquito Program's own release (https://www.worldmosquitoprogram.org/en/news-stories/media-releases/wolbachia-dramatically-reduces-dengue-cases-peer-reviewed-and), not an independent source. Trial follow-up was 27 months, so long-run durability in Yogyakarta is not independently verified here. The programme's Yogyakarta page returned 404.

title: Singapore's house-to-house dengue control
mode_reason: The source says the mosquito 'repopulates the area soon after vector control operations move to another site' and that breeding sites are created as quickly as they are removed.
who: Environmental health and vector control officers who inspect premises, with public education and legal enforcement against households found breeding mosquitoes.
does: Inspect homes and other premises for containers holding Aedes larvae, remove breeding sites, and penalise breeding under vector control law.
pays: Singapore government (public programme; budget not stated).
result: Programme fully in place by 1973; the share of inspected premises with larvae has since been about 2%, and Singapore had a 15-year period of low dengue incidence (Ooi, Goh and Gubler 2006).
contested: Same source: dengue has 'surged despite the low premises index' since the 1990s, and 'vector control may have worsened the dengue situation' by lowering herd immunity; the authors also fault a shift to case-reactive control.
when_it_stops: Not a full stop but a slackening: the authors link resurgence partly to 'the adoption of a case-reactive approach to vector control' in place of routine surveillance-led inspection.
quote: natural breeding habitats are created as quickly as they are eliminated
quote_speaker: Eng-Eong Ooi, Kee-Tai Goh and Duane Gubler (authors)
source_title: Dengue prevention and 35 years of vector control in Singapore
notes: Saved: singapore_eid_ooi2006.txt. The source is from 2006; current inspection numbers, later record outbreaks and Singapore's male-Wolbachia releases are not verified in this run (the National Environment Agency page did not render without JavaScript). 'Who pays' is an inference from the programme being a government unit, not a statement in the source. No officer is quoted.

title: Sri Lanka: malaria-free on the second attempt
mode_reason: Indigenous cases have been zero since October 2012 and WHO certified the country malaria-free in 2016, though the source says surveillance and screening of arrivals must continue to prevent reintroduction.
who: The Anti Malaria Campaign's regional malaria officers and their teams of public health inspectors, laboratory technicians, field officers and entomology teams, plus mobile malaria clinics.
does: Indoor spraying and other vector control, mobile clinics for prompt diagnosis and treatment in high-transmission areas, case investigation, and screening of high-risk people entering the country.
pays: The national anti-malaria campaign, with 'support from key partners such as WHO and the Global Fund' (as the source states); amounts not stated.
result: Fewer than 1 000 cases a year by 2006; zero indigenous cases since October 2012; certified malaria-free by WHO on 5 September 2016 (WHO South-East Asia).
contested: A 2019 review notes that Sri Lanka's intensive entomological surveillance drew 'questions ... about its cost effectiveness', and recounts the failed first attempt (https://europepmc.org/article/PMC/PMC6664748).
when_it_stops: In 1963 malaria was 'reduced to a mere 17 cases'; then 'financial and political commitment to eliminate the disease faltered leading to a resurgence of malaria, which lasted for the next 5 decades' (same review).
quote: It also demonstrates the importance of grass-roots community engagement and a whole-of-society approach when it comes to making dramatic public health gains
quote_speaker: Dr Poonam Khetrapal Singh, WHO Regional Director for South-East Asia
source_title: WHO certifies Sri Lanka malaria-free
notes: Saved: srilanka_malaria_who.txt, srilanka_malj_premaratne2019.txt. 'Turns' holds only with standing surveillance; the 1963 reversal is the reason to read it cautiously. The half-million-case figure for the late-1960s resurgence is from memory and not in the pages fetched. No field worker is quoted. Team composition is from the 2019 review.

title: Mexico's yearly dog rabies vaccination
mode_reason: WHO validated elimination in 2019, yet the programme is an annual mass dog vaccination (18.4 million doses in 2015) that WHO and PAHO say must continue because the virus still circulates in wildlife and across borders.
who: Vaccinators, brigade supervisors and coordinators of the national dog rabies programme, with public health services giving post-exposure treatment to bite victims.
does: Free mass vaccination of dogs every year, surveillance, public awareness campaigns and post-exposure prophylaxis.
pays: Mexican government (the cost study takes 'a governmental perspective'); vaccination is free to owners.
cost: Incremental cost of MXN 4,700 million (USD 300 million, 2015 prices) for 1990-2015; about USD 23,000 per human rabies death averted (González-Roldán et al., PLoS NTD 2021).
result: Human cases transmitted by dogs fell from 60 in 1990 to 3 in 1999 and zero in 2006 (WHO); the programme is estimated to have prevented about 13,000 human rabies deaths in 1990-2015 (PLoS NTD).
contested: The cost study notes that 'the absence of dog-mediated human rabies deaths has been one of the critical criteria to keep funding', and that after elimination rabies could be reintroduced from Guatemala, Belize or wildlife (https://europepmc.org/article/PMC/PMC7963054).
when_it_stops: Not documented for Mexico in the pages fetched; WHO and PAHO recommend 'continuing all rabies prevention, surveillance and control actions'.
quote: Eliminating rabies doesn’t happen by accident
quote_speaker: Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, WHO Director-General
source_title: Mexico is free from human rabies transmitted by dogs
notes: Saved: mexico_rabies_who.txt, mexico_rabies_pmc7963054.txt. Mode goes against the 'certified free' reputation on the evidence of continuing annual campaigns. A news report of later suspected dog-linked human cases appeared in search results but the page returned 403, so it is not verified. No vaccinator is quoted. Pin is the state named for the last two human cases.

title: Tsetse fly eradicated from Zanzibar
mode_reason: Sterile-male releases ran from August 1994 to December 1997 and then stopped; the last wild fly was trapped in 1996 and cattle screened since have stayed free of the disease on this isolated island.
who: Zanzibar's agriculture ministry, the tsetse research institute in Tanga that reared the flies, pilots who released them, and field teams checking more than 500 traps and sentinel cattle, with the IAEA and FAO.
does: Suppressed flies with insecticide pour-on treatments on livestock, then released 8.5 million sterile male flies by light aircraft twice a week and monitored traps daily to weekly.
pays: Government of Tanzania, IAEA, FAO and donors including Belgium, Canada, China, Sweden, the United Kingdom, the United States, IFAD and the OPEC Fund (as the source states).
cost: Programme cost not stated; annual losses from the cattle disease before eradication were estimated at 2 million USD.
result: Last indigenous fly trapped in week 36 of 1996; more than 3,000 cattle screened in 1998-1999 were all negative for trypanosomosis (Vreysen et al., PLoS NTD 2014).
contested: No criticism found in the pages fetched. The authors themselves stress that success depended on 'the complete isolation of the target population' and warn that programmes lacking such prerequisites are likely to fail.
when_it_stops: Releases stopped in 1997 by design and the disease has not returned; the source does not report any reinvasion.
quote: None of the animals were found positive for AAT, and this has remained so ever since.
quote_speaker: Marc Vreysen, Khalfan Saleh and colleagues, FAO/IAEA and Zanzibar agriculture ministry (authors)
source_title: Sterile Insects to Enhance Agricultural Development: The Case of Sustainable Tsetse Eradication on Unguja Island, Zanzibar, Using an Area-Wide Integrated Pest Management Approach
notes: Saved: tsetse_pmc4038469.txt. This is a livestock disease (nagana, 'AAT' in the quote), not a human one. The account is written by the implementers; no independent evaluation or published criticism was fetched, and IAEA web pages returned 403. A 2015 survey confirming the island still tsetse-free appeared only in search results and is not verified.

title: Turnaway Study of abortion denial
place: San Francisco, California (University of California, San Francisco)
mode_reason: The study compares women who received a wanted abortion with women turned away just past a clinic's gestational limit, and finds that this one event separates years of different poverty, employment and public-assistance outcomes.
who: Researchers at the University of California, San Francisco, who interviewed the women by telephone twice a year for five years; the women were recruited at 30 abortion facilities across the United States.
does: Follows women who presented for abortion just before or just after a facility's gestational limit in 2008-2010 and compares what happened to those who received an abortion and those who were denied one.
pays: Research and institutional grants from the Wallace Alexander Gerbode Foundation, the David and Lucile Packard Foundation, The William and Flora Hewlett Foundation and an anonymous foundation (as stated in the article).
result: Among 813 women, those denied an abortion who gave birth had higher odds of household poverty six months later (adjusted odds ratio 3.77), lower odds of full-time employment (0.37) and higher odds of receiving public assistance (6.26) than women who received one; the differences stayed significant for 4 years and 'gradually converged over the 5 years' (Foster et al., American Journal of Public Health, 2018; self-reported interview data). A separate analysis linking the same women to credit reports found 'a large increase in financial distress that is sustained for several years' among those denied (Miller, Wherry and Foster, NBER working paper 26662, 2020, revised 2022).
contested: Limits stated by the authors: the participation rate was 37.5%, many women did not know their household income, and the sample is from the United States in 2008-2010 only. David Reardon of the Elliot Institute argues in Linacre Quarterly (2018) that 'over 68 percent of the women they sought to interview refused' and that results were selectively reported: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6161227/ . The study team answers that 'these rates are well within the expected range for a five-year study' and that outcomes did not differ between high- and low-participation sites: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9755483/
when_it_stops: This is the study of what happens when the abortion is refused: higher odds of poverty, less full-time work and more public assistance for about four years; the authors add that public assistance 'did not keep households of women denied an abortion from living in poverty'.
quote: Women denied an abortion were more likely than were women who received an abortion to experience economic hardship and insecurity lasting years.
quote_speaker: Diana Greene Foster and co-authors, University of California, San Francisco (the article's conclusion)
source_title: Socioeconomic Outcomes of Women Who Receive and Women Who Are Denied Wanted Abortions in the United States
source_publisher: American Journal of Public Health (full text on PubMed Central)
notes: This entry is evidence about the act, not a service. ANSIRH's own website (ansirh.org) returned HTTP 403 in this run, so the study's own peer-reviewed article was used. The fetched article lists the authors at UCSF in San Francisco; 'ANSIRH' and an Oakland address are not in it, so the pin is UCSF. Only the socioeconomic paper, the NBER abstract, one critique and one reply were opened; the study's mental-health and physical-health papers were not opened and are not reported here. Files: turnaway_ajph2018.txt, nber_w26662.txt, turnaway_reardon2018.txt, turnaway_commentary2022.txt.

title: Abortion funds after Dobbs
place: United States (national network of nearly 100 independent local funds)
mode_reason: The funds pay and arrange travel caller by caller, and the network reports requests doubling since 2022 while nearly a third of funds paused their hotlines when money or staff ran out, so the support has to be raised and given again for each person (the abortion each caller obtains is the bounded act; see the Turnaway entry).
who: Nearly 100 independent abortion funds that answer hotlines, supported by the National Network of Abortion Funds with grants, leadership development, infrastructure support and technical assistance.
does: Pay towards the cost of abortions and give practical support such as gas money, hotel stays and childcare to people who call.
pays: not stated (the release asks for donations and 'deep investment' but does not list funders)
cost: About $396 per abortion seeker supported in 2025, up from $188 in 2022 (NNAF, 2025 survey).
result: Callers supported rose from 82,000 in 2022 to 158,000 in 2025, while requests rose from about 117,000 to about 234,000 (NNAF 2025 Membership Enrollment Survey, 97 funds responding; self-reported by the funds).
contested: No independent evaluation was opened. The figures are a survey by the network of its own members, and by those figures support reached 158,000 callers against about 234,000 requests; the release says 'The need is growing even faster than available resources'. https://abortionfunds.org/2025-membership-enrollment-survey-press-release/
when_it_stops: Nearly a third of abortion funds said they had to pause their hotlines 'due to funding shortages, staffing burnout, legal barriers, security concerns, and political attacks' (NNAF release of 1 June 2026 on 2025 data).
quote: Abortion funds are doing everything they can to meet the moment
quote_speaker: Poonam Dreyfus-Pai, Interim Executive Director, National Network of Abortion Funds
source_title: 2025 Membership Enrollment Survey: Press Release
notes: Pinned at country level on purpose (the coordinates are only the middle of the contiguous United States); no local fund, clinic or individual caller is named. The only person named is the network's public spokesperson. The 2024 survey release and the 2025 data sheet were also saved. Files: nnaf_mes2025_press.txt, nnaf_mes2024_press.txt, nnaf_mes2025_pdf.txt.

title: Socorristas en Red abortion accompaniment
mode_reason: The network's own 2014-2025 series counts people informed and accompanied year after year (9,011 in 2025), and the work has continued since the 2020 law; the law, which the network says it helped win, is the turn, and the accompaniment is given again for each person.
who: Volunteer feminist activists organised in autonomous local collectives across Argentina, who describe their work as voluntary and solidary activism.
does: Give information that follows World Health Organization protocols and accompany people who have decided to end a pregnancy, whether they go through the formal health system or not.
pays: not stated (the network describes itself as voluntary activism)
result: Information given to 109,175 people between 2014 and 2025; 9,011 in 2025, of whom 5,356 (59.4%) were accompanied through what the network calls the community health system and 2,118 (23.5%) through the formal health system (Socorristas en Red's own records, published June 2026, with data support from the Universidad Nacional del Comahue).
contested: No external criticism of the network was opened in this run. The figures are the network's own records, not independently audited. The same report says its formal-health-system figures since 2023 must be read against national and provincial policies that are dismantling public health care: frozen salaries, abortion-care teams breaking up, supply shortages ('desabastecimiento de insumos') and renewed obstruction by some professionals. https://socorristasenred.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/06/Sistematizacion-2025.pdf
when_it_stops: not stated for the network itself; for public provision, the report describes frozen pay pushing professionals out, abortion-care teams being taken apart and supplies running short since 2023.
quote: Nuestros principios dan cuenta de un activismo voluntario y solidario.
quote_speaker: Socorristas en Red, collective statement on its 'Quiénes somos' page
source_title: Sistematización de acompañamientos a abortar realizados por Socorristas en Red durante el año 2025
source_publisher: Socorristas en Red (feministas y transfeministas que abortamos)
notes: Safety: abortion has been legal in Argentina since 30 December 2020 (Law 27.610, as the network states) and the network publishes openly; pinned at country level only. The local collectives' phone numbers and addresses on the website, and the names of the report's authors, are deliberately not reproduced, and nothing is said about how accompaniment is carried out. The quote is from https://socorristasenred.org/quienes-somos/ . Files: socorristas_sist2025_pdf.txt, socorristas_quienes.txt, socorristas_home.txt, socorristas_sistematizaciones.txt.

title: Nepal legalises abortion, 2002
mode_reason: One legal change in 2002, followed by organised training and certification, was followed by a falling share of serious complications among abortion cases at four referral hospitals between 2001 and 2010.
who: By the end of 2011, over 1,200 trained and certified clinicians at 532 sites; from 2008 staff nurses and auxiliary nurse midwives were eligible to provide early procedures.
does: Provide legal abortion on request up to 12 weeks in certified facilities, with medication abortion added to the programme in 2009.
pays: not stated
result: Among 23,493 abortion-complication cases at four large public referral hospitals, the risk of serious complications fell in 2007-2010 (odds ratio 0.7, 95% CI 0.64-0.85) and sepsis fell earlier (odds ratio 0.6); 'nearly 500,000 women' obtained safe, legal abortion care by 2011 (Henderson et al., PLoS ONE, 2013). The paper cites an estimated fall in maternal mortality from 360 to 170 per 100,000 live births between 2000 and 2010 and notes 'limitations in the available data'.
contested: Limits stated by the authors: many women were still unaware of the law or wrongly believed a husband's permission was needed; women past 12 weeks without a legal indication 'may go elsewhere'; and the study is a review of hospital charts that cannot tell induced from spontaneous abortion and does not count deaths. https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3669364/
when_it_stops: The law has not been reversed, but services around it were cut: under the expanded US 'global gag rule', a 2019 Kathmandu Post and BuzzFeed News investigation found that in nearly a dozen districts 'curtailed USAID funding has led to staff reductions and the closure of clinics'. https://kathmandupost.com/health/2019/11/01/how-donald-trump-s-anti-abortion-rule-is-creating-a-dystopia-for-nepali-women
quote: The liberalization of abortion policy in Nepal has benefited women’s health, and likely contributes to falling maternal mortality in the country.
quote_speaker: Jillian T. Henderson and co-authors, a team of Nepali and US clinicians and researchers (the article's conclusion)
source_title: Effects of Abortion Legalization in Nepal, 2001-2010
source_publisher: PLoS ONE (full text on PubMed Central)
notes: The maternal-mortality figures are estimates the paper cites from other sources, not its own finding. A 2024 Devex article on aid cuts and abortion in Nepal returned HTTP 403 and was not used; effects of the 2025 US cuts in Nepal were not verified. A 2021 CREHPA policy brief on the gag rule was saved but only skimmed. Files: nepal_henderson2013.txt, nepal_ktmpost_ggr2019.txt, nepal_crehpa_ggr2021.txt.

title: Matlab door-to-door family planning
mode_reason: Field workers visited every woman of childbearing age about every two weeks with supplies and advice, for years; a 35-year follow-up found a lasting change in fertility but no lasting health or economic gain for the women themselves.
who: Community health workers in a programme run by icddr,b: village women who were married, had eight or more years of education and used contraception themselves.
does: Home visits offering a choice of pills, condoms, foam tablets or injectable contraceptives (later the IUD), with maternal and child health services added over time.
pays: not stated for the programme (the 35-year follow-up study was funded by the US National Institute on Aging and others)
result: Fertility fell about 15 percent in programme villages compared with control villages by 1982, a gap that persisted to 1996 (Joshi and Schultz, IZA Discussion Paper 2639, 2007). Thirty-five years on, among 1,820 women, the programme had 'significantly increased contraceptive use, reduced completed fertility, lengthened birth intervals, and reduced age at last birth' (Barham et al., PNAS, 2021).
contested: The same 35-year follow-up found the programme 'had no significant positive impacts on health or economic outcomes' for the women, and modestly poorer overall health in the programme area; this conflicts with the more favourable Joshi and Schultz paper. The authors note that assignment was by block, not randomised, and that the comparison area received services after about a dozen years. https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8409382/
when_it_stops: Not documented for Matlab itself. icddr,b, which runs the site, terminated over 1,000 employees after the US suspended funding for foreign programmes (The Financial Express, Dhaka, 1 February 2025); whether Matlab's services were affected was not verified. https://today.thefinancialexpress.com.bd/print/over-1000-icddrb-staffers-laid-off-over-usaid-fund-cut-1738346965
quote: Field workers visited all women of childbearing age approximately every two weeks with contraceptive services, supplies, and advice.
quote_speaker: Shareen Joshi and T. Paul Schultz, describing the programme (IZA Discussion Paper 2639, 2007, https://docs.iza.org/dp2639.pdf)
source_title: Thirty-five years later: Long-term effects of the Matlab maternal and child health/family planning program on older women's well-being
source_publisher: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences (full text on PubMed Central)
notes: The quote and the description of the workers come from a second fetched source (the IZA paper), not from the PNAS article named as the main source. No voice of a Matlab health worker was found in the pages opened. icddr,b's own Matlab page could not be opened (the URL tried returned an empty page). Coordinates are approximate for Matlab upazila. Files: matlab_pnas2021.txt, matlab_iza_joshi_schultz.txt, matlab_icddrb_layoffs_fe.txt.

title: Zimbabwe mobile contraception teams cut
place: Zimbabwe (rural outreach; pinned at country level)
mode_reason: Mobile teams kept returning to remote communities to supply contraception, and when the grant ended in January 2025 the provider's own account is that services stopped, which is what maintenance looks like when it lapses.
who: Mobile health teams of Population Services Zimbabwe, the local affiliate of MSI Reproductive Choices, who were also supporting 100 public health facilities and 120 private healthcare operators.
does: Travel into remote communities to offer free contraceptive services, and sexual health information for young people.
pays: A five-year USAID grant of $9 million awarded in 2023, ended in January 2025; MSI says 50% of its overall income is self-generated, and that private donors have since funded training for 150 public health providers.
cost: $9 million over five years (USAID grant awarded 2023, as stated by MSI)
result: MSI states that the lost funding 'would have enabled 1.3 million women and girls to access reproductive health services, averting an estimated 1,400 maternal deaths' (MSI's own projection, January 2026; not independently measured).
contested: All figures are the provider's own estimates and projections; no independent audit was opened. Independent evidence on the policy mechanism: a Stanford study in The Lancet Global Health found that when the US 'Mexico City Policy' was in force, abortions in exposed African countries 'were 40 percent higher', because NGOs that lost funding also supply contraceptives. https://med.stanford.edu/news/all-news/2019/07/us-foreign-policy-to-restrict-abortion-funding-results-in-more-abortions
when_it_stops: January 2025: the programme ended so fast that 'we weren't able to give communities and clients any warning'; vehicles were confiscated, staff contracts ended and services stopped (MSI, January 2026). Earlier, under the Mexico City Policy, the organisation said it had halved its contraceptive education sessions in rural Zimbabwe (Stanford Medicine, 10 July 2019).
quote: Vehicles were confiscated and staff contracts ended. Services stopped.
quote_speaker: Country director of Population Services Zimbabwe, MSI's local affiliate (named in the report)
source_title: One year on: USAID dismantled - impacts on global reproductive rights
notes: Safety: MSI provides abortion care in other countries, but this entry covers its contraception outreach only, is pinned at country level (coordinates are the middle of Zimbabwe, not a site), and does not name the director or the provider pictured in the report. The PDF is two-column; the quote was checked against a reading-order extraction of the same download. Files: msi_usaid_report_jan2026.txt, msi_usaid_report_jan2026_readingorder.txt, msi_one_year_on.txt, gagrule_stanford2019.txt.

title: Inuit midwives bring birth home
mode_reason: Opening the maternity in 1986 ended routine evacuation to southern hospitals for one village and then for a region: CBC reports that nearly nine out of 10 Nunavik births now happen in the region and three more communities opened their own maternities.
who: Inuit midwives trained on the job at the Inuulitsivik Health Centre maternity, with midwives in training and, because of staffing gaps, midwives brought up from the south.
does: Prenatal care and birth in the community and in Inuktitut, instead of sending women to hospitals more than 1,000 kilometres away.
pays: not stated
result: More than 3,000 babies born at the Puvirnituq maternity since 1986; caesarean rate of two per cent against a national rate of just under 32 per cent (2021-22); late fetal and early newborn deaths under one per cent, 'roughly the same as the Canadian average' (CBC, 2023, reporting research by midwife-researcher Vicki Van Wagner; the underlying studies were not opened).
contested: CBC reports a staffing problem: after a 2022 retirement the clinic had three registered Inuit midwives, so southern midwives are still needed, which 'complicates the Inuit-led maternity care originally envisioned'; and 'the model has not been widely and successfully replicated beyond Nunavik'. https://www.cbc.ca/radiointeractives/thecurrent/hands-of-a-midwife
when_it_stops: The situation before 1986, and still the case in much of Canada's North: pregnant women 'must still make long journeys, often alone' to give birth among strangers and across a language barrier (CBC, 2023).
quote: It can start to heal our own communities. It can open up women’s health.
quote_speaker: Akinisie Qumaluk, retired Inuk midwife, Puvirnituq
source_title: Hands of a midwife
notes: The outcome figures are as reported by CBC, not checked against the journal articles (Van Wagner et al. 2007 and 2012 were located but not opened). Two further documents on Nunavik midwifery were saved but not used for figures. Files: nunavik_cbc.txt, nunavik_epoo2012.txt, nunavik_pmc2025.txt.

title: Comadronas, Guatemala's Indigenous midwives
place: Chimaltenango and the western highlands (national register of comadronas)
mode_reason: Comadronas care for each woman through pregnancy, birth and the weeks after, over working lives of 30 to 40 years in the cases quoted; the 2025 stipend recognises that continuing work and does not replace it.
who: More than 20,000 comadronas registered with the Ministry of Health (their national movement, Nim Alaxik, counts at least 23,000), many of them Maya elders addressed as 'abuela comadrona'.
does: Prenatal and postnatal care, attendance at births and breastfeeding support in rural and Indigenous communities, in the women's own languages.
pays: Families, rarely and often in kind (D+C, 2008); since 19 May 2025 the Ministry of Health pays registered comadronas a yearly stipend under Decree 4-2025 (AGN, the government news agency).
cost: 4,000 quetzales per comadrona per year, paid in two parts (2025, as stated by the government news agency)
result: First payment made on 19 May 2025 to more than 20,000 registered comadronas (AGN, a government source). No evaluation of health outcomes was opened.
contested: Recognition came late and was reversed once: a 2017 law granting 250 quetzales a month was vetoed by President Jimmy Morales, and the 2015 national comadrona policy was 'largely ignored' in practice (D+C, 2017): https://www.dandc.eu/en/article/difficult-birth-law-improve-situation-traditional-midwives-guatemala . A comadrona quoted by AGN says the ministry used to discriminate against and hit them. The main source is the government's own news agency.
when_it_stops: not stated; a comadrona told D+C in 2008 that state doctors and nurses almost never came to the villages and 'we are the only ones women can turn to for help'.
quote: No solo es un salario, es un reconocimiento.
quote_speaker: Martina Sansik, comadrona from Tecpán, Chimaltenango
source_title: “Después de años de discriminación, hoy nos reconocen”, comadronas reciben estipendio con gratitud
source_publisher: Agencia Guatemalteca de Noticias (AGN), the government news agency
notes: The share of births attended by comadronas was only found in a 2008 D+C article and is too old to state as current, so it is left out. A 2024 Guardian report on discrimination against comadronas could not be opened (the syndicated copy returned HTTP 403). Coordinates are for Chimaltenango, the department two of the quoted comadronas come from. title: Kangaroo mother care, Bogotá
mode_reason: A bounded period of skin-to-skin care in the first weeks was still associated with differences in IQ, home environment and behaviour 20 years later among the trial's most fragile infants; the care itself still has to be given baby by baby, so this is the less clear-cut of the 'turns' entries.
who: Mothers, and in some families fathers, who carry the infant skin-to-skin, with the health teams of kangaroo programmes; Fundación Canguro, a non-profit, researches the method and trains teams.
does: Continuous skin-to-skin contact, exclusive breastfeeding when possible, and early discharge with close follow-up for preterm and low-birth-weight infants.
pays: not stated for the care; the 20-year follow-up study was supported by Grand Challenges Canada and COLCIENCIAS (Colombia).
result: Twenty years after a 1993-1996 randomised trial in Colombia, among 264 participants who weighed 1800 g or less at birth, the effects on IQ and home environment 'were still present 20 years later in the most fragile individuals', with less school absenteeism, hyperactivity and aggressiveness in the kangaroo group (Charpak et al., Pediatrics, 2017). Fundación Canguro says it has trained health teams in more than 40 countries (its own website).
contested: No independent criticism was opened in this run. Limits stated in the paper: 441 participants (62% of the original trial) were re-enrolled and 264 analysed, the lasting effects are reported for the most fragile infants, and some earlier differences were no longer significant 'because of loss of statistical power due to attrition of the cohort'. The study was led by the foundation that promotes the method. https://portaldeboaspraticas.iff.fiocruz.br/wp-content/uploads/2018/10/peds.2016-2063.full_.pdf
when_it_stops: not stated
quote: This study indicates that KMC had significant, long-lasting social and behavioral protective effects 20 years after the intervention.
quote_speaker: Nathalie Charpak and co-authors, Fundación Canguro, Bogotá (the article's conclusion)
source_title: Twenty-year Follow-up of Kangaroo Mother Care Versus Traditional Care
source_publisher: Pediatrics (American Academy of Pediatrics), DOI 10.1542/peds.2016-2063; full-text copy hosted by Fiocruz's Portal de Boas Práticas
notes: The URL is a hosted copy of the published article, not the journal's own site. No parent's or nurse's voice was found in the pages opened, so the quote is the authors'. The two-column PDF was checked against a reading-order extraction of the same download. The foundation's claim of children benefited is not reproduced because the counter on its home page rendered as zero in the fetched text. Files: kmc_charpak2017_pdf.txt, kmc_charpak2017_pdf_readingorder.txt, canguro_home.txt.

title: Hamlin fistula hospitals, Ethiopia
mode_reason: A fistula repair is a bounded operation with a reported 94% closure rate in 2024/25, and UNFPA describes a repaired patient returning to the same centre years later to give birth safely.
who: Surgical teams at the Addis Ababa Fistula Hospital and five regional fistula centres, and graduates of the Hamlin College of Midwives working in rural health centres.
does: Surgery for obstetric fistula and pelvic organ prolapse, rehabilitation and reintegration, and midwifery support to more than 80 rural health centres to prevent the injury.
pays: International partners, donor organisations, local companies and individual donors (annual report); whether patients are charged nothing was not verified in the pages opened.
result: July 2024 to June 2025: 4,119 surgical procedures across Hamlin's centres, of which 879 were fistula or fistula-related operations (325 at Addis Ababa); fistula closure rate 94% and cure rate 81% (Hamlin Fistula Ethiopia's own annual report).
contested: No external evaluation was opened; the data are self-reported. By the report's own figures prolapse surgery makes up a large part of the total, the cure rate (81%) is below the closure rate (94%) and slightly down on the year before, and the report cites difficulty identifying fistula patients. https://hamlinfistula.org/wp-content/uploads/2022/12/Annual-Report-2024-25-.pdf
when_it_stops: No funding cut is documented in the pages opened. The report attributes the lower number of surgeries at its Bahir Dar centre to 'escalating security challenges', and monthly dips to security problems and travel restrictions.
quote: Every woman healed is a story of hope restored.
quote_speaker: Dr Mengistu Asnake, Chair of the Board of Trustees, Hamlin Fistula Ethiopia
source_title: Hamlin Fistula Ethiopia Annual Report July 2024 - June 2025
notes: A UNFPA Ethiopia article (27 January 2025) gives a different total, 4,272 surgeries and a 93% closure rate 'in 2024', a calendar year rather than the report's fiscal year. That article names a patient; her name is not reproduced here. The claim that care is free of charge is widely repeated but was not found in the fetched pages. Coordinates are approximate for the hospital in Addis Ababa. Files: hamlin_ar2024_25.txt, hamlin_unfpa.txt.

title: Mentor Mothers, mothers2mothers
place: Cape Town (headquarters; terminated programmes were in Lesotho, South Africa and Zambia)
mode_reason: Mentor Mothers support each pregnant woman and client through continuing contact, and when the contracts behind them were terminated in early 2025 the number of people reached fell 49% in a single quarter.
who: Local women living with HIV, employed as community health workers called Mentor Mothers.
does: Peer support and primary health services for women and families, including prevention of mother-to-child transmission of HIV.
pays: United States Government awards until they were terminated in 2025, alongside other donors and the organisation's reserves (as m2m describes it).
result: Mother-to-child HIV transmission of 0.6% among enrolled clients in 2024, and over 12,000 jobs created for women living with HIV since 2001 (m2m's own figures).
contested: No independent evaluation was opened; the figures are self-reported. m2m's first-quarter 2025 report says that because of the disruption 'we were unable to calculate our usual outcome and impact metrics'. https://m2m.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/04/2025QR_Q1_NoFinancials.pdf
when_it_stops: After the US award terminations of early 2025, people reached fell from 278,213 in the last quarter of 2024 to 141,052 in the first quarter of 2025; over 650,000 people in Lesotho, South Africa and Zambia lost access to m2m services; and hundreds of frontline workers, 'almost all of whom are African women living with HIV', were laid off (m2m, April 2025).
quote: We were told to immediately stop working, without prior notice.
quote_speaker: Chichi Chilikwela, Mentor Mother in Zambia
source_title: Can't Stop. Won't Stop: m2m's commitment to health for all
notes: The Mentor Mother is named because m2m publishes her name and role itself. The pin is the headquarters named in the quarterly report; the work is spread across several African countries. Later 2025-2026 updates on how many Mentor Mothers returned to work were not opened. Files: m2m_aid_cuts_2025.txt, m2m_q1_2025.txt, m2m_home.txt, m2m_wont_stop.txt.

title: Birthing in Our Community, Brisbane
mode_reason: The service gives antenatal and midwifery care for each pregnancy, and the measured gains (fewer preterm births, more antenatal visits, more breastfeeding) are rates that depend on the service continuing; setting it up in 2013 was the one-off change.
who: Midwives and staff of a partnership between the Institute for Urban Indigenous Health, the Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Community Service and the Mater Mothers' Hospital.
does: Indigenous-led, culturally safe maternity care for First Nations families, established in 2013 on Yuggera and Turrbal Country.
pays: not stated; the researchers say Aboriginal Community Controlled Services 'need Federal Government help to access insurance and Medicare'.
result: Preterm births '50 per cent less likely', an almost 40 per cent increase in breastfeeding after discharge and an 80 per cent increase in women attending more than four antenatal sessions, comparing 766 women in the service with 656 in standard care over seven years (Charles Darwin University release on Kildea et al., The Lancet Global Health, 2021).
contested: The trial was non-randomised, as its title says. The figures above are the university's press-release wording; the journal article returned HTTP 403 and was not opened, so the adjusted estimates are not verified. At publication the service covered only Brisbane's south. https://www.cdu.edu.au/news/indigenous-birthing-services-vital-health-mothers-and-babies
when_it_stops: not stated
quote: National policy recommends Birthing on Country services be tested – now we have the evidence of their benefits
quote_speaker: Yvette Roe, Professor in Indigenous Health, Charles Darwin University
source_title: Indigenous birthing services vital to health of mothers and babies
notes: A press release by the lead authors' university, not the paper itself. The page's photo caption shows a woman who is both a participant and a midwife in the programme; she is not quoted. Whether the service has since expanded was not verified. File: australia_bioc_cdu.txt.

title: Afghan midwifery schools closed
mode_reason: Midwifery is given birth by birth and its workforce has to be renewed by training new cohorts; the December 2024 closure of midwifery institutes stops that renewal, which the midwives' confederation says threatens to undo the progress of twenty years.
who: Afghan midwives, whose number grew from 467 in 2002 to 6,376 in 2020, with their own national professional association.
does: Attend births and care for mothers and newborns; until December 2024 midwifery institutes trained women to do so.
pays: The public health system 'was largely funded by foreign aid for nearly two decades' (RFE/RL).
result: Maternal mortality fell from 1600 per 100,000 in 2002 to 638 per 100,000 in 2019 while the number of midwives rose (International Confederation of Midwives, citing a 2023 report by the Afghan Midwives' Association and UNFPA; the statement says 'accompanied by', an association and not proof of cause).
contested: The Taliban's Public Health Ministry claims access to health care has improved, says about 200 mothers died in childbirth 'last year' and puts some deaths down to missed check-ups (RFE/RL, 12 August 2026): https://www.rferl.org/a/afghanistan-healthcare-maternal-mortality-taliban-kabul/33827032.html . The 2023 report behind the confederation's figures was not opened.
when_it_stops: On 3 December 2024 the Taliban authorities ordered midwifery and nursing institutes closed, banning women from the training. UNICEF, as reported by RFE/RL, says Afghanistan could lose up to 5,400 female health workers by 2030; RFE/RL also reports that the health system has been 'in freefall' since international donors cut funding in 2021.
quote: Banning women from studying midwifery threatens to undo all the progress made.
quote_speaker: International Confederation of Midwives (statement)
source_title: ICM Statement Condemning the Ban on Afghan Women Accessing Midwifery Education
notes: No Afghan midwife or student is named here, although RFE/RL quotes some by first name. The confederation says the order came from the Taliban authorities; this run did not open an official Taliban text of the order. Files: afghanistan_icm.txt, afghanistan_rferl.txt.

title: Kraamzorg postnatal home care
place: The Hague (national service; the petition was handed to parliament)
mode_reason: A maternity carer comes to the home in the eight days after every birth, and where carers are short families get the minimum hours or none at all.
who: Kraamverzorgenden (maternity carers), about 9,500 nationally with a shortfall of about 1,500 in 2023, whose work is checked by midwives.
does: Care for mother and baby at home in the eight days after birth: checks, weighing and measuring, breastfeeding support and household tasks, about 42 hours per family on average and at least 24 (NOS, 2023).
pays: not stated in the pages opened
cost: not stated for the service; carers' standby pay is around €11.50 per eight-hour shift before tax (DutchNews, 2025).
result: not stated (no outcome evaluation was opened)
contested: Five unions say the service 'is under threat due to a severe shortage of labour and inadequate pay'. The employers' body Bo Geboortezorg planned fewer hours for a second child from 2025 and online care to fill gaps, which a midwife quoted by NOS regards with scepticism. https://nos.nl/artikel/2485973-kraamzorg-noodgedwongen-heringericht-minder-zorg-bij-tweede-kind
when_it_stops: Unions say 500 families did not get a maternity carer at home 'last year' (2024), and the FNV cites research projecting 37,000 families without kraamzorg within 10 years, 'a quarter of all births' (DutchNews, 17 June 2025).
quote: For your confidence, it is essential…And there is no alternative in the Netherlands
quote_speaker: Yvette de Vries, spokeswoman for the FNV union
source_title: Kraamzorg carers call for better pay to combat shortages
notes: News sources only; no ministry, insurer or outcome study was opened, so who pays and what the care achieves are not stated. The quote is from a union spokeswoman speaking as a mother, not from a carer. The NOS article is dated 9 August 2023. The pin is the parliament's city, chosen only to place a national service.
